ABSTRACT: Large Language Models (LLMs) have a vast capacity for thinking and reasoning and can interact with the real world as agents, but they are segmented and lack integrated systems for validating thoughts and actions like humans. This limitation often results in LLMs falling into the trap of "Local Optima" in task performance. To address this issue, we introduce a Replanning mechanism for LLM-based agents that dynamically integrates feedback from actions and implicit information which not available in an initial thinking and reasoning framework, forming a bridge between the thinking and acting of LLMs. Compared to other agent methods, experiments conducted on real-life ticket booking websites such as Ctrip and Booking show that our method is more robust in executing clear instructions, capable of successfully completing more steps, and achieving a higher success rate in practical tasks such as ticket booking. especially in challenging tasks that require interactive thinking and action for LLMs.

Existing agent methods fail to fully integrate the behaviour of
Large Language Models (LLMs) into a unified process of reasoning
and action. [13] This limitation prevents LLMs from rethinking
based on global information with implicit information, especially
when they encounter errors. They can only correct their actions
based on error messages about the current state. In attempting to
revise their plans, they do not proactively acquire implicit informa-
tion that was not previously considered. Instead, they simply iterate
and correct errors by putting all action information and feedback
received into the LLM’s prompt, thereby falling into the trap of
"local optima" in task performance. For example(Fig. 1A), in the
React method [42], LLMs progressively receive external feedback
and base their thinking and actions on the current information,
thus initiating cycles of feedback, thinking and action. Action in
the current step is based solely on thinking about the feedback for
that step. If a problem arises at an intermediate step, such as the
lack of cabin class information in the example, it will continue with
the missing information and get stuck. Voyager [33] and Reflexion
[24] are two methods that can partially address these shortcomings.
Voyager considers both feedback from the current environment and
error information to reconstruct the current action. Reflexion uses
the entire process of one or more steps as feedback for correction,
to some extent taking into account a broader set of information.

We spread the explicit information in the text along the log-

2METHOD:
This paper discusses the thinking and action paradigm of the Large
Language Model (LLM) based on implicit expression and Replan-
ning. The capabilities are primarily contributed by three new com-
ponents: (1) logic path reasoning based on KG (Sec 2.1); (2) single
action process incorporating environmental feedback and skill man-
agement (Sec 2.2); (3) task chain management for implementing
Replanning and Reaction (Sec 2.3).

2.2 A single action process based on

environmental feedback and skills
management

To enable the interaction of Replanning and Reaction in LLM’s
actions, LLM’s single action must be manageable, generalisable,
and adjustable throughout the planning process. [15, 21] We treat
LLM’s single action as a dynamic skill management system based on
environmental feedback. For example, when a flight booking task

(1) Environmental Awareness: Real-time web environment in-
formation, including web text, interactive elements, and corre-
sponding HTML, is integrated into the dynamic action process
of LLM. The cleaned web page text and interactive components
are used as inputs to LLM, which then selects the origin, desti-
nation, and time to be triggered.

(2) Skill library management: Once the current task and inter-
active elements have been clarified, LLM queries a skill library
to check for directly applicable skills. This library is managed
by a vector database that embeds vector keys describing the
skill’s applicable scenarios and input information. The values
are Python Selenium scripts for triggering web operations. If
the relevant skill exists, LLM will execute the script, receive
real-time web information as feedback for the next action.
(3) Error handling mechanism based on environmental feed-
back: Section three introduces a global error handling mecha-
nism that involves Replanning and Reaction strategies based
on task chain management. Furthermore, to prevent random
errors during the single skill creation process, such as errors
in code generation, an error handling mechanism based on en-
vironmental feedback has been established. When an error is
encountered, the code interpreter provides feedback, and the
environmental awareness mechanism is re-invoked to check

We also use a vector database to store different task chains.
These chains are merged based on the vector similarity of the tasks,
creating a comprehensive mindmap that encompasses multiple
task chains. This mindmap dynamically integrates and manages
actions triggered in the past, following the logical relationships
of the planned tasks. When similar or identical tasks need to be
performed again, there’s no need to rebuild the plan or call skills
for each action. Path matching quickly retrieves similar or identical
chains of tasks, and by using the Reaction method, multiple steps
are executed at once. This approach not only reduces the likelihood
of random errors in complex tasks involving multiple interactions,
but also significantly reduces the time and token consumption
required for LLM reasoning. This method increases the efficiency
and accuracy of task execution, enabling the LLM to handle complex
tasks more intelligently and effectively, reducing error rates and
processing time, and improving overall system performance.

2.3 Task chain management
2.3.1 Replanning. Although we’ve designed an iterative error-
handling process for single actions in Section 2.2, when errors
occur due to lack of information, it’s essential to introduce new
information on a global scale to reconstruct the plan. For example,
if the original plan did not take into account the selection of aircraft
seats, and the task fails after two iterations on the current page, a
Replanning mechanism is introduced as follows(Fig. 5):

(1) Task chain generation: Concatenate the [current task, ac-
tion execution state, next task] triplets from the start to the
point of failure into a single task chain. The action execution
status includes the skill called or created, input values, success
status and feedback received. This task chain not only provides
a complete process flow, but also has the ability to integrate
multiple actions into a single sequence of operations from top
to bottom.

(2) Replanning: Replanning the single task chain by introducing
implicit information enables the LLM to identify missing infor-
mation from the task chain and create a workable plan. This
allows corrections and resumption of the task chain from the
point of interruption.

This approach ensures that the LLM can adapt and respond
flexibly and efficiently in complex and dynamically changing task
environments, ensuring successful task completion.

3.2 Baselines
To achieve multi-round interactions on real web pages, LLM agents
need to receive feedback from the environment and call APIs mul-
tiple times to obtain reasoning about the task and generate code
to interact with the environment. Not every agent method is com-
patible with such a complex process. Our goal is to compare the
performance differences between different agent methods when

interacting with real web pages based on instructions, due to dif-
ferences in reasoning and action modes. Therefore, for the sake of
fairness, we have done our best to select and adapt some represen-
tative algorithms as benchmarks.

React [42] uses chain-of-thought prompts[47] to advance to the
next task based on a [think, act, observe] process. We provide it
with environmental feedback from our website and agent state as
observations. The action stage provides executable skills generated
on Ctrip.com as tools for use, and when instructions requiring
implicit information are encountered, the knowledge base is passed
as a pre-prompt.
Reflexion [24], which is similar to React [42] in its execution
logic, includes a module that can reflect on and correct the trajec-
tory of task completion. We recorded the trajectory of the task
execution and provided it to Reflex when errors occurred so that
it could correct the errors.
VOYAGER [33] has a skill library module for generating and stor-
ing executable code, and a mechanism for handling code errors
based on iterative prompts. To minimise the impact of random
errors in code generation, in addition to VOYAGER’s own gen-
eration of executable code, we also provided VOYAGER with an
executable skill library generated on Ctrip.com for comparison.

data structures [43], it enables LLMs to retrieve available knowl-
edge and generate more robust plans. At the action level, the agent
approach provides LLMs with specific skills and tool manipulation
capabilities that allow them to influence and shape the environment
based on their thought processes and provide feedback. The React
[42] framework provides a method for obtaining environmental
information by observing and updating state actions, and some
methods allow clues from task completion or post-action obser-
vations to help correct action errors. For example, the reflexion
[24] design allows for iterative modification of action trajectories;
VOYAGER [33] provides a specialized toolkit (skill library) that
allows LLMs to perform actions in specific domains and correct
errors through environmental feedback; some methods advocate
human-agent interaction, allowing them to correct some errors
and use such feedback to modify action errors. However, these
reasoning-based agent methods also have their potential draw-
backs. Agent-generated plans often lack awareness of common
sense knowledge gained from real-world exploration and implicit
information gained from deep reasoning about facts, leading to the
formulation of unachievable plan [7], such as "How to build a naval
fleet in Mongolia". Therefore, our method details how to transform
the thought-driven action agent paradigm into a dynamic inter-
active process in which thought guides action, action generates
new knowledge, new knowledge integrates implicit knowledge,
and guides further reasoning and planning.

map to integrate all the information. By exploiting the symbolic
understanding capabilities of LLMs, it enables LLMs to perform
highly personalised and accurate planning.

shown to stimulate the reasoning abilities of large language models
